And this is why I believe the FBI is either behind the times, or truly evil. If you have physical access to the phone, and you only what access to that phone, you do not need a universal software solution.

Yeah the encryption key is stored somewhere in memory. There has to be some unencrypted application that runs to decrypt the phone so it can be used and that application has to use the Key which is also not encrypted and in the phone's memory.

Are you familiar with hashing? When you log into a website, usually the website does not store your password but instead runs it through a hash algorithm to get something else. So the hashed password is stored, but that won't work as a valid password because the login process will try to hash it again. Salting may be another method used by iPhones.

This only helps with authentication (is the password entered by the user correct?), not encryption. To decrypt you are at some point going to need to actually use the contents of the key, not just check that it is correct.

So hashing (with a salt) only applies to protecting that part of the key which the user enters manually every time they unlock their phone. You will only have to brute force the passcode and not the encryption key. And this is only if they properly use the passcode as part of the encryption key. If they don't, you could likely just skip the code that checks the passcode versus the hashed+salted copy.

Hashed passwords are more of a client/server thing where you don't want passwords to get leaked. If an attacker has access to the code they could just skip the hash.
